persona.who: 39, Indian-American, two kids, runs a dental practice with her husband, loses her temper with the kids and hates herself after.
persona.note: I yelled at my 7 year old this morning for spilling milk and the look on his face. I am turning into my mother. I run a practice, I manage 12 people calmly, and then at home I just snap

understanding.emotion: ashamed and afraid of becoming her mother
understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call anger that takes over, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: By the end of the week the split between work and home is named, the anger is seen as a signal, and you take back the first quiet hour of your day.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the snap and the shame, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the anger is not who you are, but a mind with nowhere to land.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the calm you hold at work is real, and the snap at home is not the measure of you.
week_beats.act: You try one quiet hour before the next day, and one honest word to your son.
week_beats.story: A woman who snapped and then chose to give herself the first quiet hour of her day shows you what rising again looks like.

understanding.core_struggle: A working mother who manages twelve people calmly at work but snaps at her seven-year-old at home, terrified she is becoming her own mother.
understanding.mirror: You hold twelve people steady all day, and the minute you get home the milk spills and you snap.
understanding.insight: It is not that you are becoming your mother. It is that your mind has no quiet place left to land, and the moment you get home it has nowhere to go but out.

queries.hook: The shame of snapping at the one person you love most, and the terror that the calm you hold all day is not who you are.
queries.diagnose: Anger rises from blocked wanting, and a mind with no quiet place to land turns on the nearest person; blocked wanting is what snaps at the end of a day with no hour of your own.
queries.steady: Praise and blame come and go, and the mind that has been pulled in every direction all day is not the measure of who you are.
queries.act: Give yourself one quiet hour before the next day begins, and speak to your son about the spill before you let the morning begin again.
queries.story: A woman who held a household together, lost her temper, and then chose to give herself the first quiet hour of her day.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः । स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥
verse.line: Anger clouds judgement, clouded judgement loses memory, lost memory wrecks reason, and then you fall.
verse.translation: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from confusion of memory, the ruin of understanding; and with understanding ruined, a person is lost.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.
verse.misuse: Not 'never feel anger'. It warns about anger that takes over judgement, not about naming wrongs.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady mind looks like. Krishna tells him that when you dwell on what angers you, anger clouds your judgement. Once judgement is clouded, memory falters, and with it, your understanding of what is right and wrong. That is when you fall. The verse says that steadiness is built by guarding what you give your attention to. Anger is not the first step. It is what comes after you have already let your mind sit on a wound.
verse.for_you: You manage twelve people at work without a raised voice. At home, the same mind snaps at your seven-year-old. The split is not who you are.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: श्री भगवानुवाचकाम एष क्रोध एष रजोगुणसमुद्भवः । महाशनो महापाप्मा विद्ध्येनमिह वैरिणम् ॥
verse.line: It's desire, which turns into anger when blocked. Never satisfied, it is the real enemy here.
verse.translation: The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the quality of passion; all-devouring and greatly harmful. Know this to be the enemy here.
verse.why: Desire unmet becomes anger; see it clearly and you can master it.

prasang.title: Restraining desire
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks why we do wrong as if forced. Krishna names desire, which turns into anger, as the enemy that clouds wisdom like smoke over fire, and tells him to master it.
prasang.lesson: Desire unmet becomes anger; see it clearly and you can master it.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after he asks what force drives a person to commit wrong against their own will. He says that desire is the root cause. When a desire is blocked or unfulfilled, it becomes anger. This anger is born of passion and is like a fire that consumes everything. It is the true enemy that clouds the mind and leads to ruin.
verse.for_you: At work, desire is met and things run. At home, the quiet is broken, and that unmet need for rest turns into the snap. The anger is not your nature. It is a signal that the mind has no place to land. Let it be a signal, not a verdict on who you are.

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: Rules of conduct for a renunciant.
verse.sanskrit: नात्यर्थं सुखदुःखाभ्यां शरीरमुपतायेत् । स्तूयमानो न तुषेत निन्दितो न शपेत्परान् ॥
verse.line: Don't wear out your body chasing pleasure or fleeing pain. Praised, don't gloat; blamed, don't curse others.
verse.translation: Let him not torment the body too much for the sake of pleasure or pain. Praised, let him not gloat; blamed, let him not curse others.

verse.meaning: A teacher is speaking to a student who has left home to seek truth. The student has likely been pushing their body hard, punishing it through fasting and extreme discipline. The teacher stops them. You are not meant to wear your body out. This applies to pleasure and pain alike. When praise comes, do not swell with pride. When blame comes, do not turn that heat toward others. The teacher is saying that the anger you feel at home is not a failure of character.
verse.for_you: You manage twelve people with a steady hand. That calm is not a mask. It is a real skill. When you get home and the tension turns on your child, see it as your body asking for rest, not as proof you are becoming your mother. Let the work self rest without judgment.

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: न हृष्यत्यात्मसंमाने नावमानेन तप्यते / गाङ्गो ह्रद इवाक्षोभ्यो यः स पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Don't swell with praise or burn at a slight; stay deep and still like a river pool.
verse.translation: One who is not elated when honoured, nor pained when slighted, and who stays unruffled like a deep pool of the Ganga, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.
prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.meaning: King Dhritarashtra is awake in the dark, heavy with dread before the peace talks. His half-brother Vidura comes to sit with him. Vidura tells him that a wise person does not swell with praise or burn at a slight, but stays unruffled like a deep river pool. This is the mark of someone who can decide calmly and act steadily.
verse.for_you: The calm you keep with your twelve people at work is real. The snap at your seven-year-old is not the measure of you. You are not becoming your mother. You are just a river pool with no deep water left.

verse.speaker: Lakshman
verse.setting: Lakshman, continuing his night talk with Guha, after comparing the world to a dream.
verse.sanskrit: अस बिचारि नहिं कीजिअ रोसू। काहुहि बादि न देइअ दोसू॥ मोह निसाँ सबु सोवनिहारा। देखिअ सपन अनेक प्रकारा ॥
verse.line: Think it through: don't give way to anger, and don't blame anyone needlessly.
verse.translation: Thinking this through, do not give way to anger, and do not blame anyone without reason. Everyone is asleep in the night of delusion, and in sleep they see dreams of many kinds.
verse.why: Before blaming someone for your pain, look at the whole chain of causes, including yourself.
verse.misuse: Not blaming is not the same as excusing harm.

prasang.title: Lakshman and Guha by the sleeping Ram
prasang.summary: On the first night of exile, Guha the boatmen's chief sees Ram and Sita sleeping on grass and weeps with anger at Kaikeyi. Lakshman, keeping watch, tells him no one gives us joy or sorrow; we live out our own actions, so don't blame anyone needlessly.
prasang.lesson: Before blaming someone for your pain, look at the whole chain of causes, including yourself.

verse.meaning: After comparing the world to a dream, Lakshman speaks to Guha the boatmen's chief. Guha is weeping with anger at Kaikeyi for causing Ram's exile. Lakshman tells him to think it through and not give way to anger. Everyone is asleep in the night of delusion, seeing many dreams. Before blaming someone for pain, look at the whole chain of causes, including yourself. This is not the same as excusing harm.
verse.for_you: At home, the moment you walk in, your mind has nowhere to land. It is not that you are becoming your mother. It is that your mind has no quiet place left to land, and the moment you get home it has nowhere to go but out.

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Just told he is exiled, Ram calms his furious brother Lakshman.
verse.sanskrit: निगृह्य रोष शोकं च धैर्यमाश्रित्य केवलम्। अवमानं निरस्यैनं गृहीत्वा हर्षमुत्तमम्॥ उपक्लुप्तं यदैतन्मे अभिषेकार्थमुत्तमम्। सर्वं निवर्तय क्षिप्रं कुरु कार्य निरव्ययम्॥
verse.line: Rein in anger and grief, lean on your steadiness, and set the insult aside.
verse.translation: Hold back your anger and grief, lean on steadiness alone, set this insult aside and take up real cheerfulness. Quickly undo the preparations made for my coronation and get on with what needs doing, without fuss.
verse.why: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.
verse.misuse: Not a call to ignore injustice; it is about choosing your response.

prasang.title: Lakshman's fury, Ram's calm
prasang.summary: Lakshman is enraged by the injustice and wants to seize the throne by force. Ram calms him: set aside the insult, don't torment yourself, the setback may lead somewhere better. Lakshman answers that effort, not fate, decides; both views are given their due.
prasang.lesson: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.

verse.meaning: Ram has just learned he must leave Ayodhya for the forest. Lakshman is furious that this injustice has been done to him. He wants to fight, to seize the throne by force. Ram tells him to calm down. He says to rein in the anger and grief, and lean on steadiness. Set the insult aside and find real cheerfulness. Then undo the coronation preparations and get on with what needs doing, without fuss.
verse.for_you: Your son is not the enemy. When you get home, take one quiet hour before you see them. In that hour, set the day's work aside. Then speak one honest word to them about how you feel, without blaming.

story.hook_title: Lakshman stormed the gates ready to fight, and a queen stood calmly in his way
story.teaser: Lakshman stormed the gates ready to fight, and a queen stood calmly in his way
story.for_you: Tara stood in the way of a man ready to fight, and she did not flinch. She gave him reason and courtesy when he was full of rage. She knew that strong people think before they let anger take over. When you come home, the anger is already there waiting.

script: You are home, but you are not there. The guilt is already sitting on your chest before you have even finished closing the door. You are afraid of what you are becoming. That fear is heavy, and it is hard to breathe under it.

Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady mind looks like. Krishna tells him that when you dwell on what angers you, anger clouds your judgement. Once judgement is clouded, memory falters, and with it, your understanding of what is right and wrong. That is when you fall: And Krishna replied:
क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः, स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति.
In plain words: Anger clouds judgement, clouded judgement loses memory, lost memory wrecks reason, and then you fall.

This is not about never feeling anger. It is about what happens when anger takes over. The texts say that anger clouds judgement. Your mind gets a little blurry. Then you lose sight of what really matters. Your memory of who you are and what you value starts to slip away. Finally, reason goes, and you fall. This is easier said than done, because you are tired and your mind has nowhere to land. But the verse says that steadiness is built by guarding what you give your attention to.

At work you are calm. You manage twelve people and keep your voice steady. At home, your mind has nowhere to go but out. The anger is a signal that your mind has no quiet place left to rest. See it as a signal, not as the whole truth.
What are you letting your mind sit on right now?

depth.life: You run a practice and manage twelve people with a steady hand. At home, that same mind finds its only release in a sharp word to your seven-year-old. The fear of becoming her lives in that gap between the door closing and the snap happening.
depth.points: Anger does not arrive fully formed. It begins with what you let your mind chew on. When that chewing goes on too long, it clouds your sight. Then you forget why you are doing what you are doing. The ruin is not the anger itself, but the loss of your own clear seeing.
depth.practice: When you arrive home, leave your work bag by the door. For the first five minutes, sit in the car or on the steps. Do not enter the house yet. Just let the noise of the drive settle.
depth.question: What are you dwelling on right before the door closes?
